present_on_scene_date.note: THE RECORD DOES NOT REACH THE DAY. Every source that names this person falls on one side of 1 July 1835, and nothing follows them to it or says they left. `uncertain` rather than dropped — the distinction index.json draws for Jeremiah Porter, and a finding, not a gap. AND THE BRACKET THIS CARD ONCE HAD IS WITHDRAWN, NOT LOST: its at-or-before leg was tax_1833 alone. THE 1833 TAX LIST IS A PROPERTY ROLL, NOT A RESIDENCE CHECK (T-1117): it names the owner of ground inside the town, resident or not, and its own entry 110 is a man three years dead. It bounds the town's RECORD of this name and not the day this person reached Chicago, so it cannot say this person was here to be followed across the day. Withdrawn to `uncertain` and not to `absent` — no source places this person anywhere else on 1 July 1835 either, and a man who was taxed for ground in the town may perfectly well have been standing on it.

kin.note: THE MIRROR OF THE ROW ON hh_miller_john. ANDREAS NAMES THE BROTHERS IN ONE BREATH: 'John Miller, brother of Samuel, the landlord, came in 1831, and run a tannery just north of Miller's tavern' (History of Chicago vol. 1, the 1833 roster). The RELATIONSHIP is documented and this row does not doubt it. INFERRED, AND THE REASON IS THE IDENTIFICATION RATHER THAN THE TIE. Andreas prints the brother as 'Samuel, the landlord' and never with a surname; the town holds exactly one Samuel Miller — hh_miller_samuel, rung G1b, named by the 1832 muster, the Democrat and the 1833 tax list — and what ties him to Andreas's landlord is a shared surname carried by the sentence and the same three years in the same town. That is one agreement, and the crosswalk rule this project uses for a MERGE asks for a second. The trade does not supply it: hh_miller_samuel records no occupation, which is an absence rather than a disagreement, and this project's own miller_house record has the tavern 'past its innkeeping days' by the scene date. So the row is written at the grade the weakest link deserves. JOHN MILLER'S CARD SAYS SAMUEL 'is not written as a household here': that was true of the hand-authored parcel and stopped being true when the civic mint gave Samuel a card of his own, which is the card this row points at. A SECOND AND INDEPENDENT STATEMENT OF THE TIE, AND IT SUPPLIES THE SURNAME ANDREAS ELIDES. Moses and Kirkland: 'In 1831 two brothers, John and Samuel Miller, built a tannery just north of the latter's tavern near the junction of the two branches of the Chicago river', filed as bk_mose2_013 in data/research/books/claims/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v2.json. THIS ANSWERS THE WEAKNESS THIS ROW'S GRADE WAS WRITTEN FOR. Andreas prints the brother as 'Samuel, the landlord' and never with a surname, which is one agreement where the crosswalk rule this project uses for a merge asks for a second; Moses and Kirkland print BOTH forenames against the surname, in a different compilation by different authors, and agree with Andreas on the year, the tannery and the tavern it stood north of. THE GRADE DOES NOT MOVE. Moses and Kirkland 1895 is a compilation like Andreas 1884 and neither is a record of the family, so the identification is better supported and still reasoned, and this row stays inferred. Read by tools/spend_book_kin.py (T-1320).

dated_bounds.note: PROPERTY, NOT PRESENCE (T-1117). Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 names the owners of ground inside the town, resident or not — its entry 110 is Alexander Wolcott, who had been dead since 25 October 1830 — so this row bounds what this person was assessed for and says nothing about where the person was. tools/assert_tax_roll_ruling.py holds that ruling on the two readings it rests on. THE IDENTITY IS INFERRED AND THE PAGE IS NOT. The reading of the roll is documented — the town's own paper, held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository, twice mediated by Schulz's transcription and Genealogy Trails' republication, which this project has not gone behind. What no source states is that the man on the roll is the person on this card: data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json joins them on a name, by its rule “one resident of the surname 'Miller' agrees with the entry's forenames; 3 bearer(s) of the surname were considered.”, and forenames agree initial for initial: entry 'Samuel Miller' against resident 'Samuel Miller'. A bound whose subject is inferred is an inferred bound. No grade moves here and the identity is neither reopened nor hardened.

appearance_bounds.source_title: Fifth census of the United States, 1830 — the division headed 'Peoria & Putnam Counties & Territory attached'
appearance_bounds.identity_rule: Surname and given name both agree between the 1830 reading 'Samuel Miller' and the town person 'Samuel Miller' in household hh_miller_samuel. The 1830 line is carried as EARLIER EVIDENCE for that person and grades nothing on its own.
appearance_bounds.note: A BOUND ON PRESENCE IN A DISTRICT, AND NOT AT CHICAGO. The division is headed 'Peoria & Putnam Counties & Territory attached' and the schedule never writes the word Chicago — the Fox River and Du Page settlements are inside it — so this row bounds presence in that district in the summer of 1830 and puts no body in the town, which is why `here_by` is null. The record's own note says it first: 'Presence in that district in the summer of 1830; not a Chicago residence, and never an 1835 one'. Under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 a source EARLIER than the scene date corroborates and dates and never promotes, and a source LATER than it does not promote either. THE IDENTITY IS INFERRED AND THE PAGE IS NOT: the leaf is read scan_verified off the federal schedule, and what no source states is that the head of family on it is the person on this card. data/research/census_1830/resident_crosswalk.json joins them on a name agreement and says in terms that it grades nothing on its own. No grade moves here and the identity is neither reopened nor hardened.

persons.note: THE LADDER'S OWN READING OF THIS EVIDENCE. Read from muster_1832, tax_1833. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1c), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. muster_1832 names this person at Chicago by 31 December 1832 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1). THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Miller, Mrs. Sarah | Profession. | February 25, 1874. | Dismissed.” (second_presb_0710, printed page 195), admitted 1874-02-25 by profession. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Miller' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins S. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a_married_womans_entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Miller, Samuel” (tax_1833_075, line 127). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Miller' agrees with the entry's forenames; 3 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).
